object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged event tracked by the organization, arising from an alert and/or customer ticket.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, format INC-<sequence>, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence. ... Unique. And we never delete incidents

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification from the monitoring platform (including manually raised ones) that can indicate an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an alert, from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket that can indicate an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a support ticket.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical impact/blast radius classification of an incident, SEV1-SEV4.

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer urgency classification of an incident, P1-P4.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as incident commander.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A team that owns a service (standing assignment).

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service that can be affected by an incident, owned by exactly one team.

ambiguities.description: Person identification: the incident commander is described only as 'named' with no stated identifier scheme (e.g., employee ID vs. name). Using person_name as reference_mode may not be unique across the organization -- needs clarification.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Team identification: no explicit identifier scheme discussed for Team beyond implied name; needs confirmation that team name is unique and stable.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Whether severity/priority changes over time should be modeled historically. The current model only captures current severity/priority; the timeline of changes is mentioned but not structurally captured (no Timeline/Event entity defined).

source_references.excerpt: Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' state mentioned by Owen is explicitly rejected as a formal state by Nadia and the facilitator, but it's unclear if this informal usage should be tracked separately as metadata since people 'treat it as a state.'

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: Cause classification for customer-misconfiguration incidents is explicitly parked/undecided -- no classification concept exists in the model yet pending decision by Ravi.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a decision here today? ... The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate chain acyclicity is stated as the intended rule but explicitly not enforced in practice, and two-deep chains have been observed. This constraint may need to be modeled as a 'soft'/business rule rather than a hard database constraint.

source_references.excerpt: But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Relationship between Severity/Priority correlation with SEV/P categories was discussed as independent, but the exact business meaning of 'independent' (no constraint at all vs. weak correlation) isn't fully formalized -- confirmed as no constraint needed, but worth flagging for stakeholder sign-off.

source_references.excerpt: Are they correlated at all? ... The point stands either way -- they're independent.

ambiguities.description: Manual alerts (raised by an engineer noticing something) are described as 'still an alert' and get an alert record, but it's unclear if there's a distinct sub-type or flag distinguishing manual vs monitoring-platform-generated alerts, which could affect the AlertId identification scheme (does it come from the monitoring platform for all alerts, including manual ones?).

source_references.excerpt: An engineer's looking at a dashboard for another reason and spots something. ... If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.
